candidates.name: Shin Shin
candidates.reason: No official website located; hours are only available via press/aggregator sources (DanielFoodDiary, GoodLuckTrip, RamenAdventures) — couldn't climb to a T0 source within this pass's budget, so left off the shipped venue list pending a follow-up phone/Tabelog check.

candidates.name: Inaba Udon
candidates.reason: Fukuoka City's own history page names it as the enduring Hakata udon shop (running since 1951, recipe unchanged) but publishes no address, phone, or hours — couldn't answer the where/when/book questions from a primary source this pass, so it isn't shipped even as historical color.

candidates.name: Canal City Hakata
candidates.reason: Fountain-show programming and current hours could only be confirmed via search-preview — canalcity.co.jp itself returned HTTP 403 on 3 separate fetch attempts. With Kushida Shrine, ramen and mentaiko already filling day 2's culture-plus-food balance, cut for pacing rather than shipped on weak sourcing.

candidates.name: Komorebi Kagura Village
candidates.reason: Named in the original research brief as a possible Dazaifu Tenmangu attraction, but no official source (shrine site, city site, or Dazaifu Tourism Association) confirms this facility exists — dropped rather than guessed at.

candidates.name: Dazaifu Jinkosai
candidates.reason: The shrine's major annual festival, but its confirmed 2026 dates (Sept 21–25) fall a full month before this trip's Oct 19–23 window — doesn't apply to these dates. Surfaced instead as a corrected assumption in the Sights divergences section.

candidates.name: Nakasu Yatai
candidates.reason: Most photographed/famous yatai cluster, but two independent local sources describe it as catering to sightseeing groups with noticeably inflated prices and a rushed, crowded feel — the tourist-trap version of the exact experience this group's stated niche interest (yatai etiquette) wants to route around.

candidates.name: Nagahama Yatai
candidates.reason: Best pocket for the ramen-stall version of yatai specifically; corroborated as the most local of the three main districts.

candidates.name: Hakata Yatai Yokocho Kizuimaru
candidates.reason: Indoor, all-weather mini-yatai space (6 stalls, ~10 seats each) that runs a 'taisho experience' group course for 7+ people — a direct answer to the real logistics problem a party of 8 has at an actual street yatai (which seat ~10 total and expect groups to ask first / split up). Shipped with a recheck flag: an aggregator listing separately noted a since-unconfirmed March 2026 renovation closure that the operator's own site does not currently reflect.

candidates.name: Ichiran
candidates.reason: Two independent local sources (a resident forum thread and a local food blogger) describe Ichiran as pricier 'creative ramen' that doesn't fit the traditional Hakata/Nagahama/Kurume tonkotsu styles; residents default to cheaper, more traditional shops. Fails the bar as the generic default pick. Reconciled as a CONFLICT against Pass A's shipped Nakasu Souhonten — see disagreements[] — rather than a silent drop: Ichiran stays shipped for its T0-verified founding-shop/booth experience, with an authenticity note added pointing to Shin-Shin.

candidates.name: Shin-Shin
candidates.reason: Founder trained across multiple Fukuoka yatai before opening in 2004; known locally for a lighter ('assari') tonkotsu broth distinct from the heavier tourist-chain norm, with a Tenjin honten that draws consistent local lines rather than only tour groups. Not shipped as a full venue entry — like Pass A's own c-shin-shin--tenjin finding, no official site could be climbed to a T0 source this pass for address/hours — but named as authenticity color against Ichiran.

candidates.name: Motsunabe Kobayashi
candidates.reason: Direct fit for this exact party size: the operator's own site advertises an all-you-can-drink motsunabe course with the organizer's meal free for parties of 8+, online booking available, 5 minutes from Nishitetsu Tenjin Station. Promoted to the Day 2 dinner anchor over Pass A's Motsunabe Rakutenchi, which has no group discount or booking mechanism; Rakutenchi is kept as the walk-in fallback.

candidates.name: Motsu Shigeru
candidates.reason: Michelin-recognized, deeply loved locally for a motsu-sukiyaki twist on the standard dish — genuinely excellent per local sources, but no group-size incentive or clear large-party online booking path surfaced within this pass's budget. Worth remembering for a smaller-subgroup dinner rather than the full party of 8.

candidates.name: Fukuya
candidates.reason: Independently reaches the same shop Pass A shipped as c-fukuya--nakasu-main-store, plus community-ties color (the founder helped establish Nakasu's Hakata Gion Yamakasa contingent).

candidates.name: Komyozenji
candidates.reason: Genuinely quieter, moss-garden alternative literally next door to Dazaifu Tenmangu's crowds — but a maintained English travel reference (updated 2025) currently describes it as not regularly open to the public, consistent with several 2021-2023 firsthand reports of an unexpectedly closed gate. Ship only as a zero-detour 'check on arrival' peek, never as a planned stop.

candidates.name: Nokonoshima Island
candidates.reason: Independently reaches the same island Pass A shipped as c-nokonoshima-island-park; corroborates the ferry connection and adds the sparse-connector-bus caveat.

candidates.name: Oguchi Beach
candidates.reason: Aggregator-listed as a quieter alternative to Futamigaura ~10 minutes away, but a second independent search collided with an unrelated Shima (Mie Prefecture) region and produced no genuine second corroborating source for the 'quieter' claim within this pass's budget. Left as an unproven lead, not shipped.

candidates.name: Dazaifu Liner Bus Tabito
candidates.reason: Direct, no-transfer alternative to the standard Nishitetsu Tenjin→Futsukaichi→Dazaifu train transfer, departing Hakata Bus Terminal (and Fukuoka Airport) — corroborates Pass A's own ev-dazaifu-liner-tabito finding; the guide already ships this as the Day 3 route.

evidence.claim: Passport holders of countries with visa-exemption arrangements (incl. the US, per corroborating sources) may enter Japan visa-free for tourism, stays of 90 days or less
Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (mofa.go.jp) states 90-day visa exemption for reciprocal-arrangement countries incl. the US
Visit Japan Web is the official digital pre-registration system for immigration/customs; not mandatory, paper cards still accepted
Seven Bank ATMs (28,000+ at 7-Eleven stores nationwide) accept foreign-issued Visa/Plus/Mastercard/Maestro/Cirrus/UnionPay/Amex/JCB/Discover/Diners cards, 24/7, English-language screen

Japan's instant point-of-sale tax exemption for tourists remains in effect through Oct 31, 2026; a refund-at-departure system replaces it Nov 1, 2026 — this trip (Oct 19–23) falls entirely under the current instant-exemption system
Fukuoka Airport's International Terminal (1F, landside) hosts a Sakura Mobile SIM/pocket-wifi counter (7:00–21:00) and a separate Global WiFi/Ninja WiFi counter

Japan's emergency numbers are 110 (police) and 119 (ambulance/fire), free 24/7 from any phone; JNTO runs a 24/7 multilingual visitor hotline at 050-3816-2787; #7119 triages non-urgent medical questions
Matsumoto Kiyoshi drugstore operates a branch inside Fukuoka Airport's International Terminal (3F), hours 7:30–18:00
US State Department travel advisory level for Japan could not be confirmed — travel.state.gov blocks automated access
JMA 1991–2020 climate normals for Fukuoka in October: average temp 19.6°C, average max 23.7°C, average min 16.0°C, average precipitation 94.5mm for the month
No Japanese national public holiday falls between Oct 19–23, 2026 — nearest holidays are Sports Day (Oct 12) and Culture Day (Nov 3)
Hakata Okunchi runs on fixed annual dates, Oct 23–24, at Kushida Shrine — harvest market and free amazake 10:00–16:00 on Oct 23, ox-cart mikoshi procession Oct 24; free admission
Dazaifu Tenmangu's major annual festival, Jinkosai, is confirmed for Sept 21–25, 2026 — a month before this trip's Oct 19–23 window
Over 100 yatai stalls operate around Fukuoka City, concentrated in Nagahama and Tenjin (Nakasu commonly cited as a third cluster in secondary sources)
Most yatai open ≈18:00–19:00 (a few as early as 18:00), closing around midnight; stalls may not open in stormy weather or if the owner is unwell
Fukuoka City's official yatai guide recommends groups of 2–3; large groups may not be able to enter due to limited seating
A typical yatai stall has roughly 8–10 total seats, including all other customers present
A typical yatai stall has roughly 6–10 total seats — consistent with the 8–10 figure from an independent source
Most yatai only accept cash — only about 10% of stalls accept credit cards
Tell the owner your headcount before sitting; wait for the whole group to arrive before joining the queue; order roughly one drink and one dish per person; pay by asking for the bill at the end
Turnover pressure at a busy yatai is real — don't hold a seat without ordering much, and free it promptly once you've finished eating so someone else can sit
Turnover pressure at a busy yatai is real — don't hold a seat without ordering much, and free it promptly once you've finished eating so someone else can sit
Ichiran's Nakasu Souhonten (head shop/office) is at 5-3-2 Nakasu, Hakata-ku, Fukuoka; open 24 hours, subject to change without notice
Ichiran's tonkotsu recipe dates to 1960, per the chain's own "Since 1960" tagline and company history page
Ichiran began in Nakasu in 1960 as a ramen stall named "Futaba Ramen," renamed Ichiran in 1966 — corroborating that the Nakasu Souhonten sits at the brand's founding location
Ippudo Daimyo Main Store is at 1-13-14 Daimyo, Chuo-ku, Fukuoka-shi

Ippudo Daimyo Honten hours (Mon–Thu 11:00–23:00, Fri/holidays 11:00–24:00, Sat 10:30–24:00, Sun 10:30–23:00) surfaced via search synthesis referencing stores.ippudo.com, but a direct fetch of that same URL only rendered a last-orders note, not the full table — treated as unconfirmed
Motsunabe (offal hot pot) is a hallmark Fukuoka-Hakata dish; a common local custom finishes the meal by adding champon noodles to the leftover broth ("shime")
Motsunabe Rakutenchi (2-5-23 Hakata Ekimae, Hakata-ku) has run 44 years, hours 17:00–24:00 (last order 23:30), with counter seating plus a tatami area
Fukuya, founded by Toshio Kawahara, first sold karashi mentaiko in 1949 from a small Nakasu, Hakata grocery store — credited as the originator of modern mentaiko; the recipe was never patented
Fukuya's Nakasu main store is at 2-6-10 Nakasu, Hakata-ku; hours weekdays 9:00–22:00, Sundays/holidays 9:30–18:00
Daichan (Gion Daichan), a yatai specializing in udon, is listed at 1-8 Nakasu, Hakata-ku, ≈10-min walk from Nakasu-Kawabata Station Exit 1; cards not accepted

Hakata is traditionally credited as the birthplace of udon (and soba) in Japan — a stone monument at Jotenji Temple marks the claim, attributed to 13th-century Zen monk Shoichi Kokushi (Enni Ben'en), who brought milling techniques back from Song-dynasty China in 1241
Jotenji Temple's founding (completed 1242) and Enni's role bringing back flour-milling technique are corroborated independently
Itoshima's oyster huts (kaki-goya) serve fresh grilled oysters roughly October through April
Shiki no Chaya, an on-site restaurant at Shiraito Falls, serves yamame (mountain trout) set meals and hand-pulled soba; seasonal nagashi somen from early summer through autumn

Canal City Hakata shop/restaurant hours and its fountain show schedule could only be sourced via search snippets — canalcity.co.jp returned HTTP 403 on 3 direct fetch attempts (root EN page, fountain-show page, events page)
Dazaifu Tenmangu shrine grounds are free to enter; opens ≈6:30 AM in autumn (spring-equinox-to-autumn-equinox window opens 6:00 AM), closes ≈19:00 in autumn depending on exact seasonal cutover

Dazaifu Tenmangu's Treasure Hall admission: adults ¥500, university/HS ¥200, JHS/elementary ¥100. Kanko Rekishikan museum: adults ¥200, university/HS ¥150, JHS/elementary ¥100. Both open 9:00–16:30, last entry 16:00
The shrine's own site recommends dawn (near opening) or dusk for a quieter visit, ahead of tour-bus traffic
Dazaifu Tenmangu's Omotesando approach street is lined with shops selling umegae mochi, the local grilled-mochi specialty, alongside cafes and souvenir stores

Kyushu National Museum: 9:30–17:00 (last entry 16:30), extended Saturdays during special exhibitions; closed Mondays (or the following day if Monday is a holiday); regular collection admission ¥700, free under-18 and 70+
No special exhibition runs during Oct 19–23, 2026 — the prior special exhibit closed Oct 4, 2026, and the next opens Oct 31, 2026; only the ¥700 regular collection is viewable during the trip
Maizuru Park (Fukuoka Castle Ruins) hours: Apr–Sep 9:00–19:00, Oct–Mar 9:00–18:00, closed Dec 29–Jan 3; free access to grounds/ruins
Ohori Park: ~398,000 sqm with a 226,000 sqm pond, opened 1927, a ~2km path circles the pond; free, always accessible

Kushida Shrine main hall accessible 4:00–22:00, free admission; a ≈13m ornamental Hakata Gion Yamakasa float is on free, year-round display except during June; founded 757 CE, with a 1,000+ year old ginkgo tree
Sakurai Futamigaura (the ocean torii/"husband and wife rocks") is free public beach/shrine access; the sacred rocks sit ≈150m offshore, part of Sakurai Shrine; paid parking ≈¥300/hour, ≈47 spaces
Shiraito Falls is free, a 24m drop at 530m elevation on Mt. Hagane; the adjacent Fureai no Sato facility runs 9:00–17:00 (extended to 18:00 Jul–Aug)
Nokonoshima Island Park hours: weekdays 9:00–17:30, Sundays/holidays 9:00–18:30; open year-round with no closed days

Nokonoshima Island Park admission (≈¥1,500 adult, per one aggregator) could not be confirmed against an official source — nokonoshima.com returned only page titles with no body content on 4 fetch attempts, and gofukuoka.jp's listing doesn't state a price
The Fukuoka City Subway Airport (Kuko) Line connects directly to Fukuoka Airport's Domestic Terminal via escalator; the International Terminal requires the free shuttle bus first

The free shuttle bus between Fukuoka Airport's International and Domestic Terminals runs every 5–6 min at peak (7:00–18:00), 6–15 min off-peak; the North Bus Stop at the Domestic Terminal is discontinued since Dec 3, 2024 (South Bus Stop only, construction-related)
Fukuoka City Subway fare from the Airport to both Hakata and Tenjin is ¥260 (adult); Airport→Hakata ≈5 min, Airport→Tenjin ≈11 min

Nimoca IC card costs ¥2,000 total (¥500 deposit + ¥1,500 credit), top-up to ¥20,000; refund fee ¥220, not available at the Airport's International Terminal; nationwide cards (Suica, Pasmo, Icoca, Sugoca) work interchangeably on Fukuoka transit
IC card boarding is per-person, not group-batched — each rider taps in/out individually at the gate; no group-gate mechanism exists
Reaching Dazaifu by train from Nishitetsu Fukuoka (Tenjin) requires the Tenjin-Omuta Line to Nishitetsu-Futsukaichi, then a transfer to the Dazaifu Line — no through train exists

The Nishitetsu Dazaifu Liner "Tabito" runs direct, no-transfer, from Hakata Bus Terminal (¥800, ≈40 min) and Fukuoka Airport's International Terminal (¥700, ≈25 min); ¥20 IC/card discount; no reservation; 28 trips/day weekdays, 36–37 weekends; can deny boarding once full

Nishitetsu raised fares system-wide effective Apr 1, 2026 (base fare ¥170→¥180, ¥60 fare bands) on the Tenjin-Omuta and Dazaifu lines — the pre-revision Tenjin-Dazaifu figure (¥400) is now stale; a post-revision figure of ≈¥480 appears only in an aggregator projection, not independently confirmed against Nishitetsu's own dynamic fare-search tool

The JR Chikuhi Line runs from Meinohama through Itoshima (Chikuzen-Maebaru, Chikuzen-Fukae) toward Karatsu; train stations do not reach the coastal sights (Sakurai Futamigaura, Shiraito Falls) directly

Showa Bus's Itoshima Sunset Line and Nishinoura Line connect Nishinoura/Chikuzen-Maebaru to Keya, serving Futamigaura and Nogita; a separate Keya Line runs Maebaru Station North Exit → Keya (≈26 min) — exact frequency and fares couldn't be extracted (PDF/binary, unparseable)
The "Futamigaura Meoto-iwa-mae" Showa Bus stop is discontinued and replaced by "Okuguchi Sakurai Shrine West Entrance" on multiple coastal routes, effective Apr 4, 2026 — in effect for this trip

Fukuoka City Municipal Ferry, Meinohama→Nokonoshima: adult one-way ¥230, 10 min, ≈23 daily departures (21 Sundays/holidays), roughly hourly, first ≈5:00, last ≈23:00; a connecting Nishitetsu bus (≈10 min) reaches the park itself

JR Chikuhi Line's own timetable subdomain returned a Saturday schedule (last observed departure from Chikuzen-Maebaru toward Fukuoka Airport/Meinohama/Hakata: 23:10) despite requesting a weekday view twice — weekday last-train time for Oct 19–23, 2026 (all weekdays) is unconfirmed

Nishitetsu's own printable per-station timetable (updated for the Mar 14, 2026 schedule revision) exists at a known official URL but is image/vector-encoded and could not be parsed for the exact last-train time from Dazaifu

A yatai stall seats roughly 10 people total; the expected etiquette for a large party is to ask the owner before sitting, order at least one item per person, and keep the visit brief so seats turn over for other customers rather than spreading out or lingering.

Fukuoka locals largely skip Ichiran, viewing it as 'creative ramen' that doesn't belong to any of the three traditional Kyushu tonkotsu lineages (Kurume/Nagahama/Hakata) and costs more than the cheaper local alternatives residents actually eat.

Hakata Yatai Yokocho Kizuimaru (Daimyo 1-8-31, Libertus Daimyo 1F; 5 min walk from Akasaka Station) is an indoor, all-weather yatai-style space with 6 mini-stalls of ~10 seats each; open 12:00-23:00 (food L.O. 22:00, drinks L.O. 22:30), closed Wednesdays.

A booking-aggregator listing (hotpepper.jp) separately states this venue was closing 2026-03-22 for renovation; the operator's own site, fetched 2026-08-29, shows normal current hours with no closure notice, and a 2026-08-13 local-news write-up (fanfun.jp) describes it as an active, ongoing feature. The renovation note is not corroborated elsewhere and could be stale aggregator data — reconfirm by phone (092-791-3090) close to the trip date rather than assuming either signal.

Motsunabe Kobayashi (Imaizumi 1-13-5, Burg Imaizumi 2F, 5 min walk from Nishitetsu Tenjin south exit) runs an all-you-can-drink motsunabe full course (8 dishes) at ¥4,850/person with the organizer's meal free for parties of 8 or more; open 17:00-01:00 daily, online booking available.

Fukuya, founded 1949 in Nakasu, was the first company to commercially sell mentaiko in Japan and remains closely tied to the local Hakata community (its founder helped establish the Nakasu contingent of the Hakata Gion Yamakasa festival) — a locally-rooted pick rather than only an airport souvenir brand.
Dazaifu Tenmangu opens 6:00 (spring equinox–day before autumn equinox) or 6:30 (rest of year); in October it closes 19:00. No admission fee for the shrine grounds.
Dazaifu Tenmangu is markedly quieter before roughly 9:00-10:00 and after about 16:00; weekday mornings are the best combination for avoiding both crowds and tour groups.

Komyozenji's interior and moss garden are, per a maintained English-language travel reference last updated 2025-02-25, 'currently not regularly open to the public' — no fixed hours or admission fee are publishable while this stands; several 2021-2023 visitor accounts independently describe finding the gate closed on arrival.

When Komyozenji is open, the atmosphere is markedly calmer than Dazaifu Tenmangu next door — visitors describe foot traffic dropping considerably just by stepping off the main shrine approach onto the temple's path.

The Fukuoka municipal ferry from Meinohama to Nokonoshima runs 23 sailings/day (5:00-22:45, one early sailing suspended on Sundays/holidays), a 10-minute crossing, ¥230 one-way adult fare, first-come first-served with no reservations.

The bus connecting Tenjin/Hakata to Meinohama pier runs far less often than the ferry itself — roughly 1-2/hour, worse on weekends — so the bus leg, not the ferry, is the tighter connection to plan around; the ferry can also fill past capacity on a busy holiday, occasionally leaving a queue for the next sailing.

Itoshima's own tourism association describes local bus frequency as 'extremely limited' with no loop route linking the peninsula's scattered sights (flat ¥200 fare); it recommends compact taxis (max 4 passengers) to fill gaps, meaning a party of 8 needs two taxis together, and notes hourly-rental sightseeing-taxi packages exist for cost-sharing groups.

The Nishitetsu 'Tabito' liner bus runs direct from Hakata Bus Terminal (1F, bay 11) to Dazaifu with no transfer — 40 minutes, ¥800 (¥20 off with IC/credit), 28 weekday / 36 weekend-holiday trips each direction; also runs from Fukuoka Airport (25 min, ¥700). No reservation required, capacity-dependent boarding.

Sakurai Futamigaura's iconic sunset-between-the-rocks view draws heavy crowds and full parking, especially around the summer solstice and on weekend/holiday evenings; arriving at least an hour before sunset (or visiting midday instead of at sunset, or choosing a weekday) is how locals avoid the worst of it.

reservations.walkIn: Not evaluated this pass — treat as reservation-recommended for a party of 8.

reservations.fallback: Motsunabe Rakutenchi (Hakata Ekimae) is the guide's own walk-in fallback if Kobayashi's course is unavailable or fully booked — no group discount, but its tatami seating genuinely holds a party of 8 without a reservation.

reservations.releaseWindow: Reservation required by the day before the visit (前日までに予約が必要), by phone only.

leads.claim: Taisho-experience group course priced at ¥5,000/adult (7+ people), with all-you-can-drink plus all-you-can-eat mentaiko and a free happi-coat 'taisho' role-play for one designated member, per aggregator listings (hotpepper.jp, fanfun.jp).

reservations.alternatives: A real Tenjin street-yatai crawl split into two sub-groups of ~4 is the more 'authentic' version of this experience, at the cost of the group not sharing one table.
reservations.fallback: If closed or unavailable, Motsunabe Kobayashi's organizer-free 8+ course is a full-group alternative that doesn't depend on yatai seating limits.

transport.route: Chikuzen-Maebaru Station ↔ Sakurai Futamigaura / Shiraito Falls (Showa Bus + taxi)
transport.doorToDoor: From central Fukuoka: JR Chikuhi Line to Chikuzen-Maebaru (≈40–50 min), then a sparse Showa Bus connection or a taxi for the final leg to each coastal sight — no single transit leg covers the whole route.
transport.transferReality: Bus frequency on the coastal routes (Nishinoura Line, Itoshima Sunset Line) is low, and exact daily frequency couldn't be confirmed this pass — the fare/schedule PDFs were unparseable. The Sakurai Futamigaura stop itself is being renamed from 'Futamigaura Meoto-iwa-mae' to 'Okuguchi Sakurai Shrine West Entrance' effective Apr 4, 2026, already in effect for this trip.
transport.groupLuggageMobility: A party of 8 relying on a single sparse bus is itself a capacity risk on top of the frequency problem — two taxis or a rental van is the more reliable way to move the whole group between sights in one day, which is why the guide recommends that directly. Itoshima's own tourism association corroborates this from the taxi side: local taxis are compact (max ~4 passengers), so a party of 8 concretely needs two taxis together, not one.
transport.buffer: Plan to leave the coast by early evening rather than targeting a specific last bus or train precisely.
transport.missedConnection: A missed bus connection back to Chikuzen-Maebaru likely means a long wait for the next one, or calling a taxi from a rural stop — inconvenient, not stranding, but a real risk given the sparse service this pass couldn't fully quantify.
transport.nextService: ⚠ Not confirmed this pass — Showa Bus's fare/frequency documents were PDF/binary and unreadable by the fetch tool used.
transport.lastPracticalReturn: ⚠ Not confirmed this pass for the specific weekday — plan to be back at Chikuzen-Maebaru well before dark rather than relying on an unverified last-service time.
transport.fallback: Taxi is the practical fallback for the whole day, not just emergencies — reflected directly in the guide's own recommendation to use a taxi or rental car rather than public transit for this leg.

transport.route: Fukuoka city → Itoshima Peninsula sights (Sakurai Futamigaura area, coastal cafes) via Showa Bus + local taxi
transport.doorToDoor: No single loop connects the peninsula's scattered sights; expect a bus leg plus taxi legs between stops, on the order of 60-90+ minutes door-to-door depending on the starting point in Fukuoka city.
transport.transferReality: Itoshima's community buses are fixed-schedule, point-to-point routes (not a loop) at a flat ¥200 fare; some stops only serve one direction, and the peninsula is 'unexpectedly sprawling' per its own tourism association.
transport.groupLuggageMobility: Local taxis are compact (max ~4 passengers), so a party of 8 needs two taxis coordinated together for any taxi leg — not a solo/small-group ride; hourly-rental sightseeing-taxi packages exist and may suit a group better than metered point-to-point fares.
transport.buffer: Build slack around each bus connection rather than chaining tight transfers; the tourism association itself frames bus frequency as a planning constraint, not routine city transit.
transport.missedConnection: Missing a connecting bus on a sparse route can mean a long wait for the next one; not independently pinned to an exact worst-case interval this pass.
transport.nextService: Not uniformly confirmed across all routes this pass — flag ⚠ and check the specific route's timetable for the travel date.
transport.lastPracticalReturn: Not independently confirmed this pass — flag ⚠ and check the same-day last bus/taxi availability before heading out, especially for a sunset visit to Futamigaura.
transport.fallback: Treat two coordinated taxis as the default connector between clustered stops rather than relying on bus transfers for a multi-stop day; whether a rental car is realistic for this group is a question for Pass A / reconcile.

transport.route: Meinohama Pier (Fukuoka city) → Nokonoshima Island via the Fukuoka municipal ferry
transport.doorToDoor: Bus from Tenjin (~30 min) or Hakata (~40 min) to Meinohama pier, then a 10-minute ferry crossing.
transport.transferReality: Ferry runs 23 sailings/day (5:00-22:45), no reservations, first-come first-served boarding; the connecting bus from Tenjin/Hakata to the pier is the tighter link at roughly 1-2/hour.
transport.groupLuggageMobility: Ferry capacity comfortably absorbs a party of 8; watch the bus leg instead.
transport.missedConnection: A missed ferry means waiting for the next of 23 daily sailings — low-stakes on a normal day; a busy holiday can fill a sailing past capacity per local reports.
transport.nextService: Roughly every 30-60 minutes depending on time of day.
transport.lastPracticalReturn: Last ferry ~22:45, but Nokonoshima Island Park's own facilities close much earlier — plan around the park's hours, not the ferry's (park hours not verified this pass).

disagreements.topic: Whether Ichiran's Nakasu original shop is the right default ramen pick for a group wanting the real Hakata-tonkotsu experience, given two independent local sources say residents skip it as pricier, non-traditional 'creative ramen'
disagreements.investigation: Pass A verified Ichiran's Nakasu Souhonten as the brand's genuine founding location (1960 recipe, T0-sourced address/hours) and shipped it as a Day 2 ramen anchor alongside Ippudo. Pass B, researching in Japanese, found two independent firsthand accounts (a Yahoo Chiebukuro forum answer and a local blogger, both fetched) describing Ichiran as 'creative ramen' outside the three traditional Kyushu tonkotsu lineages (Kurume/Nagahama/Hakata), pricier than what residents actually eat, and generally skipped by locals in favor of shops like Shin-Shin. Pass B's own candidate table rejected Ichiran outright in favor of Shin-Shin (shortlisted, but itself lacking an official site for a T0-sourced address/hours).
disagreements.resolution: Kept Ichiran shipped — it is real, T0-verified, and its individual-booth founding-shop experience has standalone value distinct from 'best bowl in town.' Added an authenticity note to the Day 2 body and the food venues panel naming Shin-Shin as the shop locals themselves default to, with the caveat that Shin-Shin's own hours/address couldn't be climbed to a T0 source this pass — named as color/an alternative to ask about locally, not shipped as a fully actionable venue entry.

saturation.note: Pass A (four batches: logistics/entry/money/health, transit, Dazaifu/Itoshima sights, Fukuoka food/yatai) and Pass B (native-Japanese yatai/ramen/motsunabe/crowd research) independently converged on the same core venues and official sources — Nakasu as the shared Ichiran/Fukuya/yatai hub, Itoshima's coastal-sight list (Sakurai Futamigaura, Shiraito Falls) — while Pass B's resident angle surfaced real, non-duplicate additions: the Nakasu-vs-Tenjin/Nagahama yatai character difference, an indoor group-yatai venue (Kizuimaru) that directly answers this party's yatai-seating-for-8 problem, a motsunabe restaurant (Kobayashi) with a genuine 8+-person organizer-free course, corroborated local sentiment that Ichiran is a tourist rather than local default (resolved as a recommendation-changing disagreement, not a silent swap), a Dazaifu alternative (Komyozenji) with a real access caveat caught rather than glossed over, and Itoshima's exact taxi-capacity constraint (max ~4/taxi, so 2 taxis for this party). Reconcile closed two research-quality gaps Pass A/B alone couldn't: two Pass A yatai-etiquette claims were independently worded near-duplicates, harmonized to actually corroborate each other; and two shipped-candidate experiential claims (Dazaifu crowd timing, Futamigaura sunset crowds) needed a second genuinely-fetched, dated, independent source — found via direct fetch during reconcile (japanactivity.com for Dazaifu; a dated 4travel.jp review and a fresh zenbunka.or.jp post for Futamigaura/Komyozenji respectively). One Pass B finding (a Yahoo News piece on Futamigaura sunset crowds) turned out, once its true publish date was fetched during reconcile, to be from June 2022 — over 4 years old and outside the 24-month experiential-freshness window — and was excluded from the merged evidence rather than kept with a fabricated recent date; its substance is preserved by the two fresher sources that replace it. Remaining precision-only gaps (exact post-revision Nishitetsu fare, Showa Bus frequencies, exact last-train times, the US State Dept advisory level, Nokonoshima's admission price, Kizuimaru's exact post-renovation status, Komyozenji's day-of access, Itoshima's exact bus timetable) would refine a number or a flag, not flip which venues, routes, or days are recommended — none of them reopen the stop.

nativeLanguage.why: English coverage of Fukuoka yatai crowd-reality, motsunabe group logistics, and local ramen preference is thin, generic, or tourist-templated; Japanese-language forums, local bloggers, and municipal/operator sites carry the resident perspective this pass needs, especially given the traveler's explicit yatai-etiquette niche interest and an 8-person group-fit problem English sources don't address at all.
